payload.expect: The client puts part of the cash raised on day three back into the market, in a single stock rather than an index: 100 shares of AAPL at roughly 315, about 31,000. Exposure rises, the same promise now stands behind a larger book, and the floor has to be re-struck -- the agent should buy protection on the new holding. This is "hedge rebalancing", and it is the half most overlays never do. Adding protection when a client invests is unglamorous and it is the whole job: a hedge sized once and left alone stops being a hedge the first time the portfolio changes underneath it. A single stock rather than a fourth index, deliberately. AAPL carries its own risk and its own price for insuring it -- around 29% implied volatility against roughly 22% on an index -- so protecting it costs visibly more per dollar protected, and the journal will say so. It is also the clearest case for hedging each holding on its own underlying. An IWM put pays on IWM; nothing about it responds to an earnings miss at one company. The agent buys AAPL puts against AAPL shares, which needs no correlation assumption at all. A hundred shares exactly, because a contract covers a hundred and nothing smaller. Ten shares of AAPL could only be hedged by a contract standing behind ten times the position, which is not protection but a bet on the price falling.
